--- lecture: "12a" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Foundations of]{.my-subtitle}
[Data Science]{.blue} ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | {{< meta course >}}]{}
[Jeffrey M. Girard | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ![](../../img/proud_coder_357EDD.svg){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ## Roadmap ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Understand how R handles strings and special characters - Combine, separate, and extract parts of text data - Use regular expressions to detect and replace patterns within strings ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: # Working with Strings ## Text Data in R {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - **Question:** *How does R handle text?* - Text data is stored as **strings** (character vectors) - We create strings by wrapping text in double quotes (`"as so"`) or single quotes (`'as so'`) ::: {.fragment .mt1} - We will use the \{stringr\} package (part of the \{tidyverse\}). All of its functions start with `str_` and are built specifically to handle messy text ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - We will learn the basics of regular expressions (regex) to search for complex patterns in text ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/text_box.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Creating Strings & Escapes ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we define text data in R?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- "We usually create strings by wrapping text in double quotes." writeLines(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` We usually create strings by wrapping text in double quotes. ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- "Backslashes (\\) \"escape\" special symbols, treating them as characters." writeLines(y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Backslashes (\) "escape" special symbols, treating them as characters. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- "Backslashes can also create: \nNewlines (\\n) and \ttabs (\\t)" writeLines(z) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Backslashes can also create: Newlines (\n) and tabs (\t) ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Combining Strings ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we stick multiple strings together?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble( first = c("John", "Jane", "Alice"), last = c("Doe", "Smith", "Johnson") ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 first last 1 John Doe 2 Jane Smith 3 Alice Johnson ``` ::: ::: ## Combining Strings ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How can we flexibly combine strings?* Yes, `str_glue()` lets us insert R variables directly into a string using curly braces `{}`. This is often much easier to read than `str_c()`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> mutate( greeting = str_glue("Hello, {first} {last}! Welcome back.") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 first last greeting 1 John Doe Hello, John Doe! Welcome back. 2 Jane Smith Hello, Jane Smith! Welcome back. 3 Alice Johnson Hello, Alice Johnson! Welcome back. ``` ::: ::: ## Flattening Strings ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we collapse a whole column into a single string?* We can use `str_flatten()` to combine a vector of multiple strings into one single string. We can also specify a separator. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> summarize( all_names = str_flatten(first, collapse = ", ") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 all_names 1 John, Jane, Alice ``` ::: ::: ## Real-World Application ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Which carriers operate out of each NYC airport?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data("flights", package = "nycflights13") flights |> summarize( .by = origin, # For each origin airport... carriers = carrier |> # Find its active carriers unique() |> # Remove all duplicates sort() |> # Sort them alphanumerically str_flatten(collapse = ", ") # Flatten them into one string ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 origin carriers 1 EWR 9E, AA, AS, B6, DL, EV, MQ, OO, UA, US, VX, WN 2 LGA 9E, AA, B6, DL, EV, F9, FL, MQ, OO, UA, US, WN, YV 3 JFK 9E, AA, B6, DL, EV, HA, MQ, UA, US, VX ``` ::: ::: # Extracting & Separating ## Subsetting Strings ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we extract a specific range of characters?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Hex color codes use #RRGGBB for red, green, and blue intensities df <- tibble( hex = c("#FF0000", "#00FF00", "#0000FF") ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 1 hex 1 #FF0000 2 #00FF00 3 #0000FF ``` ::: ::: ## Subsetting Strings ::: {.fs80} We use `str_sub()`, which takes a `start` and `end` position. We can even use negative numbers to count backward from the end of the string. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> mutate( red = str_sub(hex, start = 2, end = 3), # 2 from left to 3 from left green = str_sub(hex, start = -4, end = -3), # 4 from right to 3 from right blue = str_sub(hex, start = 6, end = -1) # 6 from left to 1 from right ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 hex red green blue 1 #FF0000 FF 00 00 2 #00FF00 00 FF 00 3 #0000FF 00 00 FF ``` ::: ::: ## Separating Columns ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we split one messy column into multiple clean ones?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble( id = 1:3, blood_pressure = c("120/80", "135/90", "110/70") ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 id blood_pressure 1 1 120/80 2 2 135/90 3 3 110/70 ``` ::: ::: ## Separating Columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> separate_wider_delim( cols = blood_pressure, # original/messy col name delim = "/", # character to separate on names = c("systolic", "diastolic") # new col names to create ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 id systolic diastolic 1 1 120 80 2 2 135 90 3 3 110 70 ``` ::: ::: ## Lengthening Columns ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Can we separate into rows instead of columns?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble( name = c("Alice", "Bob"), classes = c("Math, Science", "History, Art, Math") ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 name classes 1 Alice Math, Science 2 Bob History, Art, Math ``` ::: ::: ## Lengthening Columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> separate_longer_delim( cols = classes, delim = ", " ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 name classes 1 Alice Math 2 Alice Science 3 Bob History 4 Bob Art 5 Bob Math ``` ::: ::: ## Real-World Application ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Why is this useful in data science?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble(sku = c("US-APP-2023-11", "CA-BAN-2024-01")) ``` ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> separate_wider_delim( cols = sku, names = c("country", "product", "year", "month"), delim = "-" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 country product year month 1 US APP 2023 11 2 CA BAN 2024 01 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Regular Expressions ## Intro to Regex {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - **Question:** *What if our target isn't a fixed position or a simple delimiter?* - [Regular Expressions]{.b .blue} (regex) are a concise language for describing patterns in strings. They are very powerful but can look like gibberish ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Most \{stringr\} functions take in a regex pattern - We will use `str_view()` to preview what our regex is matching. Matches will be surrounded by angle brackets: `<...>` - Then we will learn how to apply them ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/search.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Exact Matching ::: {.fs80} The simplest regex pattern is just an exact match of characters. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c("apple", "banana", "pear", "pineapple") # Show me elements that contain "apple" str_view(x, "apple") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ [4] │ pine ``` ::: ::: ## Anchors ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *What if we only want matches at the start or end of a string?* We use anchors. `^` matches the start of the string, and `$` matches the end. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Show me elements that START with "a" str_view(x, "^a") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ pple ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Show me elements that END with "e" str_view(x, "e$") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ appl [4] │ pineappl ``` ::: ::: ## Regex Building Blocks ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we match flexible patterns instead of exact matches?* ::: ::: {.fs80} - **Wildcards (`.`):** Matches *any* single character - **Character Classes (`[]`):** Matches any *one* of the characters listed - **Shortcuts:** Built-in classes for common patterns + e.g., `\\d` (digits) and `\\s` (spaces) - **Quantifiers:** Control how many times a pattern repeats + `{n}`: matches exactly *n* times + `+`: matches one or more times ::: ## Examples {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c("sun", "sand", "soon", "July 4", "2026") ``` ::: :::{.columns .mt1} :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Single Wildcard str_view( string = x, pattern = "s.n" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ [2] │ d ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # One or More Wildcards str_view( string = x, pattern = "s.+n" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ [2] │ d [3] │ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Spaces str_view( string = x, pattern = "\\s" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [4] │ July< >4 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Exactly 4 digits str_view( string = x, pattern = "\\d{4}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [5] │ <2026> ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Detecting Patterns ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we filter a dataset based on text patterns?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble(name = c("Ann", "Andy", "Amanda", "Bob", "Cindy")) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 1 name 1 Ann 2 Andy 3 Amanda 4 Bob 5 Cindy ``` ::: ::: ## Detecting Patterns ::: {.fs80} We can use `str_detect()` to ask if the pattern was detected ::: :::{.columns} :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Is "an" or "An" detected? df |> mutate( match = str_detect(name, "[aA]n") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 name match 1 Ann TRUE 2 Andy TRUE 3 Amanda TRUE 4 Bob FALSE 5 Cindy FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column .fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Retain row if it is detected df |> filter( str_detect(name, "[aA]n") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 1 name 1 Ann 2 Andy 3 Amanda ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Replacing Patterns ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we fix or replace specific text elements?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (x <- "We often utilize fancy words when we could utilize simple ones.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "We often utilize fancy words when we could utilize simple ones." ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Replace the FIRST instance of the pattern only str_replace(x, pattern = "utilize", replacement = "use") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "We often use fancy words when we could utilize simple ones." ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Replace all instances of the pattern str_replace_all(x, pattern = "utilize", replacement = "use") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "We often use fancy words when we could use simple ones." ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Removing Patterns ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we delete parts of a string?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (x <- c("(555) 123-4567", "800-555-0199")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "(555) 123-4567" "800-555-0199" ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Remove any of the following: [...] # Parentheses: () # Hyphens: \\- # Spaces: \\s str_remove_all(x, "[()\\-\\s]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "5551234567" "8005550199" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Removing Whitespace ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- "\t Sometimes strings have\n too much white space " writeLines(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sometimes strings have too much white space ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Forcibly remove all whitespace str_remove_all(x, "\\s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Sometimesstringshavetoomuchwhitespace" ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Remove outer whitespace and compress inner whitespace str_squish(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Sometimes strings have too much white space" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Real-World Application ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Why is this useful in data science?* Data entered by humans in free-text fields is notoriously messy. We can string these tools together to sanitize it. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- tibble( email = c("jane AT uni DOT edu", "\njohn@gmail.com ", "educator@khan.org", "SMITH@ college.edu ") ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 1 email 1 "jane AT uni DOT edu" 2 "\njohn@gmail.com " 3 "educator@khan.org" 4 "SMITH@ college.edu " ``` ::: ::: ## Real-World Application ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df |> mutate( clean_email = email |> str_squish() |> # Collapse whitespace str_replace(" AT ", "@") |> # Replace AT with @ str_replace(" DOT ", ".") |> # Replace DOT with . str_to_lower() |> # Make all lowercase str_remove_all("\\s"), # Remove all spaces dotedu = str_detect(clean_email, "\\.edu$") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 email clean_email dotedu 1 "jane AT uni DOT edu" jane@uni.edu TRUE 2 "\njohn@gmail.com " john@gmail.com FALSE 3 "educator@khan.org" educator@khan.org FALSE 4 "SMITH@ college.edu " smith@college.edu TRUE ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
